title: Genomics, Systems Biology & Bioinformatics
text:
This course provides a conceptual and computational framework for analyzing molecular data across biological scales, from genome to transcriptome to systems-level organization.
The focus is on understanding how genetic and environmental variation influence molecular phenotypes and complex traits through modern high-throughput technologies and statistical modeling.
The course integrates biological interpretation, statistical methodology, and practical implementation in R. It is a unified framework spanning the harmonized Genomics, Systems Biology and Bioinformatics and Multi-Omics Technology in Animal Production outlines.
Use the unified course map to explore the reusable teaching blocks and the two pathways through them.

title: Genomics, Systems Biology & Bioinformatics
text:
Core Themes
The material is organized around five interconnected themes:

Molecular Technologies

DNA sequencing technologies
Genotyping platforms
RNA-seq and transcriptomics
Epigenomic and multi-omics profiling

Genomic Association and Mapping

GWAS principles
Population structure and confounding
Fine-mapping
Functional annotation

Multi-Omics Integration

Transcriptome-wide association
eQTL and regulatory variation
Integrative modeling across data layers

Systems-Level Modeling

Gene regulatory networks
Pathway analysis
Network-based interpretation
Causal modeling concepts

Computational and Statistical Methods

High-dimensional regression
Regularization and shrinkage
Machine learning approaches
Reproducible workflows in R

title: Genomics, Systems Biology & Bioinformatics
text:
Learning Objectives
After completing the course, students should be able to:

Explain how sequencing technologies generate molecular data
Evaluate appropriate statistical models for genomic data
Analyze high-dimensional datasets using R
Interpret GWAS and fine-mapping results
Integrate multi-omics datasets conceptually and computationally
Connect molecular variation to complex phenotypes

title: Genomics, Systems Biology & Bioinformatics
text:
Course Materials
The course progresses from molecular data generation to systems-level interpretation.
As the course is developed, chapters and practicals will include:

Conceptual background
Statistical framework
Applied examples
Executable R code
Visualizations and case studies

The overview and curriculum map are currently available. Slides, notes and practicals will be added in the folders described in the repository README. Students will be encouraged to reproduce worked examples and explore parameter choices as those materials become available.

title: Genomics, Systems Biology & Bioinformatics
text:
Prerequisites
Students are expected to have:

Basic molecular biology knowledge
Introductory statistics
Familiarity with R

Prior exposure to linear models and quantitative genetics is beneficial but not required.

title: Genomics, Systems Biology & Bioinformatics
text:
Recommended Use
This material is designed to support:

Lecture-based instruction
Computational lab sessions
Project-based learning
Independent exploration of genomic datasets

Emphasis is placed on connecting biological mechanisms with statistical modeling in a reproducible framework.

title: Unified course map
text:
Genomics, Systems Biology and Bioinformatics is the unified teaching framework spanning both harmonized MSc outlines: Genomics, Systems Biology and Bioinformatics and Multi-Omics Technology in Animal Production. The two outlines define different pathways through the same library of material. The unified course can also select its own sequence from that library.
Each block has one maintained explanation and worked example. A pathway chooses its depth, exercises and assessment. Shared content is revisited through a new question or a more demanding analysis when students take both courses.
This map is a curriculum design. Only the overview and this map are currently implemented; the lessons, practicals and assessments below are proposed. Original module numbering is retained in the crosswalks. Partner assignments, credit hours and assessment weights remain as specified in the supplied outlines; this map does not revise them or allocate teaching hours.

title: Unified course map
text:
Building blocks
The block numbers are stable identifiers, rather than a compulsory teaching order. Technologies can be introduced alongside the data and design decisions that make their measurements interpretable.









Block
Scope
Students should be able to
Proposed worked example or practical




B01 Foundations and biological questions
Genomics, systems biology, bioinformatics; omics layers; genotype–phenotype relationships
Define a biological question and identify the measurements needed to address it
Map a feed-efficiency question to genomic, expression, microbial and phenotype measurements


B02 Experimental design and sampling
Experimental units, biological replication, tissue and time, matched samples, collection and preservation, batch allocation
Specify a sampling design and distinguish biological effects from confounding
Compare matched and unmatched multi-omics designs; diagnose a treatment–batch confounding problem


B03 Databases and biological identifiers
Sequence, protein, structure, genome, comparative, annotation and pathway resources; identifier mapping
Retrieve and document records while preserving identifier meaning and annotation provenance
Trace a variant to a gene, transcript, protein and pathway using a small documented example


B04 Programming and reproducible data handling
R; optional command-line/Python extensions; file formats, joins, sequence manipulation and workflow organisation
Import data, verify sample identity and produce a reproducible analysis
Join phenotype and assay tables; detect swapped samples, missing identifiers and duplicate records


B05 Genomics and sequence analysis
Genome organisation, sequencing, genotyping, variation, assembly and annotation concepts; sequence similarity, alignment and phylogeny
Explain genomic measurements and evaluate basic sequence/genotype quality
Inspect sequence and genotype data; compare homologous sequences with explicit assumptions


B06 Transcriptomics
RNA-seq technologies, expression quantification, quality control, normalization, differential expression and functional interpretation
Explain an expression analysis and its design, contrasts and uncertainty
Analyse a small count dataset with biological replicates and a stated experimental contrast


B07 Epigenomics
DNA methylation, chromatin measurements, nutritional/environmental influences and regulatory interpretation
Interpret epigenomic measurements without equating association with causation
Compare regulatory measurements across tissues or conditions and identify alternative explanations


B08 Proteomics and structural information
Platforms, identification, quantification, protein structures and functional interpretation
Explain protein measurements and assess identification and quantification limitations
Explore a protein-abundance table with missing values and batch information


B09 Metabolomics
Analytical platforms, identification confidence, quantification, preprocessing and biochemical interpretation
Evaluate metabolite measurements and distinguish identified compounds from unresolved features
Examine a small metabolite panel, measurement scales and feature-identification uncertainty


B10 Microbiomics and host–microbiome relationships
Community profiling, host effects, co-metabolism, compositionality and production applications
Interpret community differences while accounting for sampling and measurement constraints
Compare rumen-community profiles with diet and host metadata; discuss relative versus absolute abundance


B11 Phenomics and precision production
Sensors, repeated measurements, high-throughput phenotyping and links to omics
Define meaningful phenotypes and account for measurement timing and repeated records
Align animal-level sensor summaries with biological sampling dates


B12 Statistical analysis and validation
Regression, multivariate analysis, multiple testing, clustering, dimension reduction, regularization and machine learning
Select an analysis and evaluate uncertainty, overfitting, confounding and leakage
Fit and compare predictive models with animal-level train/test separation and preprocessing fitted on training data


B13 Association, prediction and regulatory variation
GWAS, relatedness, population structure, fine-mapping, functional annotation, genomic prediction, eQTL and TWAS
Distinguish association, prediction and causal claims and explain their assumptions
Interpret an association region and expression evidence; assess prediction on an appropriate held-out group


B14 Pathways, networks and systems inference
Enrichment, gene regulation, protein interactions, metabolic/signalling networks and causal-model concepts
Evaluate pathway/network evidence, background sets, uncertainty and limits of inference
Compare enrichment backgrounds and assess whether a network supports a biological hypothesis


B15 Multi-omics integration
Integration strategies, sample matching, scaling, missing layers, cross-layer association and genotype-to-phenotype integration
Justify an integration strategy and interpret agreement and disagreement between layers
Integrate matched expression, protein and phenotype summaries with a documented design and validation plan


B16 Advanced and emerging methods
Single-cell, spatial omics, advanced epigenomics, 3D genome organisation and emerging AI methods
Evaluate what a new technology measures and whether it answers the study question
Critique an advanced-omics paper, separating measurement, association and mechanistic evidence


B17 Ethics, governance and research integrity
Privacy/security, sharing, open science, provenance, reproducibility and responsible AI
Specify responsible data handling and communicate analysis provenance and limitations
Write a data-management and reproducibility plan, including justified AI use


B18 Animal-production synthesis and reporting
Growth, feed efficiency, meat/milk quality, reproduction, health, adaptation, methane and sustainability
Connect a justified study design and analysis to an animal-production question
Develop an integrated case study, computational report or research proposal



B02, B04 and B17 recur throughout the course. B12 supports analyses across technologies. B18 provides applications throughout the teaching sequence, as well as a final synthesis.

Shared lessons and different extensions
Each shared lesson should have a clear entry requirement, a core explanation, a worked example, exercises with solutions and optional extensions. Reuse the same lesson when its learning objective is the same. Assign a different exercise when the objective or depth differs.

Gene identifiers, eligible background, multiple testing and interpretation

title: Unified course map
text:
Learning outcomes and assessment
The GSB outline emphasises applying computational methods, explaining association and networks, integrating data, and evaluating quality and biological significance. B03–B06 and B12–B15 provide the main analytical spine; B17–B18 support evaluation and reporting.
The Multi-Omics outline explicitly assesses distinguishing technologies, explaining collection/preservation, interpreting genomic/transcriptomic data and evaluating animal-production applications. B01–B02, B05–B11 and B18 directly support those stated outcomes. Its content also includes substantial integration and analysis in MO10–11; proposed additional outcomes would ask students to design a multi-omics study, evaluate data quality and confounding, and justify and interpret an integration strategy. These additions should be agreed before being presented as formal course requirements.

Shared practicals can use a common core rubric: correct sample/variable definitions, justified methods, reproducibility and interpretation. Pathway extensions assess additional competencies. A GSB computational report can emphasise method evaluation; a Multi-Omics proposal can emphasise sampling, technology choice and integration design. Neither project form replaces the original assessment scheme without agreement.

title: Unified course map
text:
Suggested pathways through the framework
These are teaching sequences, not allocations of credit hours. Each course can select a subset appropriate to its available time.
Unified course: introduce B01, B02, B04 and B17; survey B05–B11 alongside B03; build the analytical foundation in B12; develop B13, B14 and B15; finish with B18 and selected B16 extensions. Animal-production examples recur throughout.
GSB pathway: B01 → B03/B04 → selected B05–B07 → B12 → B13 → B14/B15 → selected B16 → synthesis and reporting. Introduce design and reproducibility as needed throughout, and use B08–B11 where they support the selected questions.
Multi-Omics pathway: B01/B02 → B05–B11 → B03/B04/B12 → B14/B15 → B18. Revisit study design before integration and use selected B13 lessons for prediction and genotype-to-phenotype relationships.
R is the primary environment for shared computational examples, consistent with the existing teaching sites. Command-line and Python exercises can be optional extensions where the original bioinformatics pathway calls for them. Software choices and dataset size should be specified when each practical is developed.

title: Unified course map
text:
Development and reuse
Keep this repository as the shared home. Use existing slides/, notes/, tutorials/, exercises/, data/, images/, R/ and scripts/ folders, with each resource labelled by its block identifier and linked from this map as it becomes available. Avoid copying the same explanation into separate course versions. Both pathways can link to one resource and assign different extensions.
Develop one complete example first: B02/B04/B06, a small RNA-seq study with sample metadata, quality checks and a biological contrast. Follow it with B12/B14 interpretation and then a B15 integration example. This connects design, computation and biological interpretation without requiring all eighteen blocks to be written first.
Existing Population Genetics, Quantitative Genetics and Bayesian Linear Regression lessons can supply prerequisites or optional background. Link to suitable lessons after checking their assumptions and level. Package integrations should use current public interfaces and should not be prerequisites until an example has been implemented and verified.
